newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major on rack again over Europe as MPs revolt.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major on rack again over Europe as MPs revolt.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's hopes of uniting his fractious party for the election fight ahead lay in tatters on Friday as a rank-and-file Conservative revolt over demands for a full debate on Europe threatened to boil over.

What started as an arcane dispute over parliamentary procedures has spiralled out of control into a showdown that, while unlikely to topple the British leader, could do grave damage to his hopes of winning a further term in office.
The row is over whether three working documents related to the European Union's plans for a single currency should be examined on the floor of the House of Commons.

Major, with a majority of just one in the 651-seat lower chamber, is anxious to avoid a full-scale debate that would doubtless reopen deep divisions over Europe that have dogged his six years as prime minister.
He drew howls of protest from his own ranks on Thursday when he insisted that the papers had been properly scrutinised by a panel of MPs that held a rowdy 2-1/2 hour meeting on Wednesday.

Euro-sceptic Conservatives with a visceral revulsion for closer European integration see the issue as a chance to promote their hostility to economic and monetary union (EMU), dominating the attention of governments throughout the European Union.
Egged on by the opposition parties, the Euro-sceptics pressed their case again on Friday under the guise of defending parliament's historic right to hold the government to account.
"Parliament should maintain its integrity and should have the opportunity to discuss these matters of absolutely crucial constitutional importance," MP John Wilkinson said.

Former Conserative leadership challenger John Redwood added: "This is an issue about proper parliamentary debate and accountability...It is a question of whether the government will debate this very important issue before granting any more powers to the Brussels institutions."

Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind warned that a rebeliion would play into the hands of Tony Blair's Labour party, in opposition since 1979, which holds a 20 percentage point lead in opinion polls with the election now less than six months away.
"The vast majority of Conservative MPs are very, very reasonable people," Rifkind told BBC radio.
"They know the Labour party are only interested in trying to exploit any differences for opportunistic electoral reasons. Conservative MPs will not want to give them that opportunity."
The squabbling is a far cry from the Conservatives' triumphant annual conference in Bournemouth last month when the party put on an impressive morale-boosting show of unity.

The Daily Telegraph said Major faced potentially the most serious challenge to his authority from ordinary "backbench" MPs. The Independent said he had embarked on a risky strategy that could plunge his government into crisis.
Major, who will see a deputation of senior backbenchers next week, is hoping a scheduled debate ahead of next month's EU summit in Dublin will take the steam out of the rebellion.
Former finance minister Norman Lamont urged the government in the interests of pre-election unity to extend that debate so the EMU documents can be scrutinised.

"The consequences of not having a debate is that there will be a lot of people very unhappy and they will try and raise the issue in other ways, and it will not lead to the public presentation of a united party, which is what we want in the run up to the election," he told BBC radio.

Opposition politicians believe Major would lose a vote on Europe. He would then have to face a motion of no-confidence the next day which, with his one vote majority, he should survive -- barring accidents.
